newsitem.title: ITALY: Rome court rejects ex-Nazi's bid for house arrest.
newsitem.headline: Rome court rejects ex-Nazi's bid for house arrest.

text.p: An Italian court has rejected a second attempt by convicted ex-Nazi Erich Priebke to be placed under house arrest in an apartment belonging to a sympathiser, the lawyer for the former SS captain said on Tuesday.

Carlo Taormina said the military court would decide where Priebke should serve his sentence for involvement in Italy's worst World War Two massacre after a tribunal had ruled exactly how long the 84-year-old should stay in jail.
Priebke was found guilty last month of participating in the mass execution of 335 men and boys in Rome in 1944 carried out in retaliation for a partisan attack on German occupying forces.
But the court granted some mitigating circumstances and other concessions, reducing the life sentence that he could have faced to five years.

Priebke's lawyers say their client has been in detention in Italy since his deportation from Argentina in 1995 and argue that he should be released on the grounds of his age and good behaviour while in custody.
The tribunal is due to rule on the request by the end of August.
Priebke is being held under house arrest in a hillside monastery near Rome, but the Franciscan order had stipulated that he should leave their care at the end of his trial.
The military court decided last week that the German should serve the rest of his jail sentence in an army hospital.
Priebke's lawyers complained that the move would jeopardise their client's mental health and posted an appeal.

Taormina said the court had again turned down a request that Priebke be moved to a house belonging to right-wing activist Paolo Giachini, but had not yet decided to enforce its earlier decision regarding the military hospital.
While the court awaits the ruling on Preibke's sentence, the head of the Franciscan monastery demanded on Tuesday that the 10-man security team guarding the former Nazi should be removed.

Father Andrea Stefani wrote to police chiefs saying that Priebke was welcome to stay: "But not the military personnel who maintain such a severe guard, which is altogether useless given Mr Priebke's complete lack of desire to flee," the letter said.
Stefani said the permanent presence of armed guards disturbed the religious life of the monastery. The police were not immediately available for comment.
